newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary govt securities yields seen down or flat.
newsitem.headline: Hungary govt securities yields seen down or flat.

text.p: The National Bank of Hungary (NBH) and government measures are seen determining yields on Hungary's government securities in the next few weeks and the yields are likely to drop or stagnate, dealers said on Tuesday.

Government bond yields -- two to five year maturities -- have dropped by 0.1-0.3 percentage points since the NBH 0.25 percent repo rate cuts two weeks ago, while discount treasury bills also declined slightly, dealers said.

The yields will drop in the next few weeks if the NBH cuts repo rates or the rates on its six-month and 12-month deposit facilities or if the government approves a planned programme for inflation reduction in 1998, some dealers said.
They said part of the market expected the NBH to cut its interest rates in the near future, perhaps this week. But other dealers remained sceptical.

"Many people still expect a substantial repo (rate) cut, but I don't think they will touch the repo," said Gabor Pozsgay, of Creditanstalt Securities, adding he saw government securities deals stagnating in the near future.
If the government approves realistic plans for 1998 inflation reduction, including a price-wage agreement, that would encourage a substantial fall in yields, Pozsgay said.
The government is expected to decide on the anti-inflationary plans on May 29.
According to the alternative programmes, year-on-year inflation may be cut to either below ten percent or to some 13 percent by December 1998, from a forecast of about 17 percent for December 1997.

The year-on-year inflation figure of 18.6 percent for April, published on Monday, was down from 18.8 in February and in March, but was unlikely to influence government security yields substantially, dealers said.
Some dealers said they expected the NBH to cut its interest rates soon, but the yields were likely to drop anyway.
"I expect a fall of some 0.25 percent within one or two weeks," said Tamas Puskas of Raiffeisen Securities.
